claims.text: Formation and crystal-structure selection in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by atomic diffusion kinetics during cooling.
Slower cooling enhances atomic intermixing by providing more time for diffusion.
Additional diffusion time allows atoms to overcome effects associated with differences in mixing enthalpy and surface-energy barriers.
Enhanced intermixing during slower cooling favors formation of a metastable single-phase solid solution.
Nanoparticles made by rapid heating followed by immediate cooling typically exhibit phase separation.
Nanoparticles made by rapid heating followed by immediate cooling typically exhibit elemental segregation.
Nanoparticles made by rapid heating followed by immediate cooling typically exhibit irregular morphology.
Cooling should be slowed after rapid heating while composition and peak temperature are held constant.
The proposed mechanism applies when constituent-element differences in mixing enthalpy and diffusion barriers are moderate.
Slower cooling reduces kinetic trapping of segregated phases.
Slower cooling promotes synchronized nucleation into a single-phase solid solution.
Relative to rapid cooling, slower cooling will produce a more uniform, single-phase crystal structure.
Relative to rapid cooling, slower cooling will reduce elemental segregation.
Relative to rapid cooling, slower cooling will produce more controlled and spherical particle morphologies.
The hypothesis may not apply when differences among the constituent elements are extreme.
The hypothesis may not apply when synthesis conditions exceed inherent thermal-decomposition limits.
The magnitude of improvement from slower cooling depends on the balance between diffusion kinetics and thermodynamic forces.
